Posted November 28, 2007 

Added comments by Richard Cowan  

(MarijuanaNews note: The first important point to notice is that the letter is necessarily anonymous. In the country we call theland of the free and the home of the brave sick, dying and disabled people too often have a choice between living in pain and living in fear.
See 

People Who Live In Pain Should Not Have to Live In Fear. In Santa Cruz, Celebrating Freedom and Denouncing A Murder.  

 

This man says, Patients should have the freedom, to choose life over death. 

 

Over the years that I have been involved in the marijuana reform movement I have become friends with many patients. I have been inspired by their courage in the face of more pain than most torture victims must endure. Indeed, when I hear good people rightly denouncing the abuse of prisoners in Guantanamo and in Iraq I want to urge them to look much closer to home. It is happening in America and Canada and the UK to people who have committed no crime except seeking relief from their intractable pain. 

See
Todd, Steve and Mike; And Why I Do What I Do.

 

Second, I have said repeatedly that marijuana prohibition has become a war on the most vulnerable members of our society. Right now, all of the frontrunnersare running away from this issue, or like Romney, Giuliani and McCain, openly hostile toward patients who challenge them. 

 

We have to do everything we can to get these people off the drug war battlefield, but ultimately we are going to have to choose between prohibition and the patients.  

See 

Note to 60 Minutes: The News Is Not That There Is Too Much Freedom In L.A., But That There Is Too Little Freedom Everywhere Else. What Is More Important, The Patients Or Prohibition?
and  
Support Our Troops Unless It Interferes with the Drug War Then Let Them Suffer and Die?? Analysis by Richard Cowan

The candidates may duck this issue, but will you?)

 

 

Dear [Presidential Candidate]: 

 

My name is J. 

 

I am 45 years old, and have been disabled with chronic pain since an on-the-job accident at a paper mill in 1992.  I am writing you in the hope that you will take a greater interest in public policy issues related to pain maintenance, OxyContin and other opiates, and the use of marijuana by patients as an alternative approach to pain management. 

 

From 1993 to 1996 I underwent 5 spinal procedures.  Aside from prescriptions for considerable levels of pain medication I have required multiple epidurals over the last 11 years to keep my left leg from losing all mobility.  My doctor tells me that in the future I will need additional surgery on the spinal region from the lumbar to the throracic, which will be an eight level fusion with hardware. 

 

I have been living with chronic pain ever since the accident.  My daily pain is not just disabling, it is in its own way imprisonment.  The side-effects of conventional pain medication has created additional side effects which have caused me to look for alternative approaches to forced dependence on opiate drugs.  I have discovered that the use of marijuana and/or related pharmaceutical products provides me with such an alternative.  The use of marijuana as an alternative to opiate drugs has produced a considerable improvement in my quality of life. (The active ingredient in marijuana, THC, triggers one of the pain reduction networks in the body that is activated by opiate drugs, but without many of the undesirable side- effects such as depression of the central nervous and cardiovascular systems.) 

 

Here is a brief review of my prescribed medication before I started using marijuana for pain management.  First I was put on Vicodin and I was taking 300 every month because the pain was so bad. Then my doctors prescribed Percocet, and then later they prescribed Levodromoran. After taking this drug for a year or more I was than introduced to a (then) new drug called Oxycontin. I was on this opiate for 7 ½ years along with another opiate called Roxicodone.  These are just the highlights.  I have also been prescribed 11 other legal drugs, including Roxicodone and Elevil.  The purpose of the prescription for Elevil, for example, was to try to short-circuit the nerve in my brain responsible for the pain I feel in my leg.  Many of these drugs either didnt work or produced additional side-effects that required additional medication.  Trial use of a spinal cord stimulator was also tried, but that didnt work for me either. 

 

While considering installation of a morphine pump that would provide a three month supply of morphine I decided to learn more about opiates.  At the web site of the American Medical Association I learned that opiates can cause Ghost or Phantom pains.  I also learned at this time that marijuana or cannabis had been used in the past both for pain relief and to help addicts get off of opiate related drugs such as heroin and morphine.  I had used marijuana before in response to depression.  Since the opiates made me so sick I decided that I needed to at least try to get off of them. 

 

My insurance company, which is responsible for my medical bills, encouraged me to consider treatment to reduce the dosage of the opiate drugs.  I wanted to go off of them completely.  I read a lot about opiates, heroin, Oxycontin, other medications and also Cannabis.  I talked to heroin addicts on the streets of SeattleWA and PortlandOR.  This, a lot of will power, and the use of cannabis has helped me to get completely off of opiate drugs for pain management.  I feel privileged to say Cannabis has saved my life   I only pray some day that I will have the freedom to be able to use my Cannabis as openly as they let me use the Opiates.

 

In my opinion Oxycontin is legal heroin.  I have accomplished getting off Oxycontin by having will power to want to live, for when I was on these Opiates all I wanted to do was rot away and die. I do believe this drug is the most dangerous drug we have in the United States. 

 

Patients should have the freedom, to choose life over death. I use only Cannabis now, and have gotten off of 13 to 14 different Pharmaceutical drugs, including the daily use of 1125 mg of opiates.  It is difficult to believe that the governments position that I have Cannabis is less safe then 1125 mg of Oxycontin or other opiate drugs. 

I have been prescribed Marinol (legally available synthetic THC), but my insurance company refuses to pay for it as it has not been approved for pain relief. I have tried to enter trial studies to obtain Sativex, a drug that they have in Canada made from Cannabis and Alcohol (which in the history books they called a tincture). Sativex would make my life so much easier, it would work, but they wont give it to me and it has not yet been approved for use in the United States (pre-approval clinical trials are underway.)  There is an administrative petition before the Bush Administration to reschedule cannabis in the United States under the Controlled Substances Act, but at best this remains a longshot and a long, drawn out administrative process that will likely end up in court.  So the only remedy left for me is to violate federal law and use Cannabis.   

 

Legal cannabis would be less expensive for me personally, or alternately, far less expensive for my insurance company.  And here is a more important public policy point for you to consider legal cannabis would be less expensive for the nation as an alternative to dangerous and costly reliance on opiate drugs for pain management. 

 

You are running for President, and here is how you can help the many patients suffering from chronic pain.  Discuss this issue in public, and contribute to the on-going public debate the medical marijuana.  Being 100% disabled to have much time to think of how our world could be and should be better. So please help change laws for ALL PATIENTS LIKE ME. 

 

Sincerely, 

 

J.
